content.title: About
content.content: Custard is a dessert made from eggs, milk, and sugar, thickened by gentle heating. It has a smooth, creamy texture and a mildly sweet flavor, often flavored with vanilla, cinnamon, or fruit purées.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Custard has been known since ancient times; the earliest recipes appear in Roman cookbooks.
Traditional English custard is made only with eggs, milk, and sugar, without any starch.
In the United States, “thickened custard” often includes corn starch for a firmer consistency.
Custard is frequently used as a filling for pies, tarts, and éclairs.
Savory custard, made with cheese, herbs, and spices, is served as a side dish in many cuisines.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs, the main ingredient, provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Milk contributes vitamin D, which supports bone health and the immune system.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Calcium from milk helps strengthen teeth and bones.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs supply B2 and B12, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Easily digestible energy source
items.content: The combination of simple carbs and protein makes custard a quick and sustained source of energy.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Traditional sweet custard contains a notable amount of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and blood‑glucose spikes.

items.title: Risk of bacterial contamination
items.content: If not heated properly, eggs may not be fully pasteurized, increasing the risk of salmonella.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consuming milk‑based custard.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Custard can be served chilled or warm as a dessert, used as a filling for pastries, drizzled with fruit, berries, or caramel sauce. It can be prepared on the stovetop, in the microwave, or in a steam bath.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared custard in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions; thaw in the fridge before serving.
